policy.core: The supplied Chapter 8 defines LO 8.1 through LO 8.5. Reading and chapter vocabulary trace to those headings, including the ethical dilemma, security, sustainability, and when-things-go-wrong discussions.
policy.supplement: Applications 8.6 and 8.7 are explicitly labeled extensions applying existing Porter frameworks and ordinary cost reasoning to original hypothetical enterprise-system decisions. They are not part of the chapter's own objectives.
policy.hypotheticals: Every numerical exhibit, firm, and practice organization is explicitly hypothetical. No invented figure is attributed to a real organization. Real companies named in the chapter are used only as the chapter uses them.
policy.currentLaw: Compliance material is taught as a reason enterprise systems record what they record. The module does not assert current legal requirements and does not offer legal advice.
policy.datedFigures: Vendor prices, market shares, license costs, adoption counts, and chapter forecasts are omitted. Vendor capabilities are taught by use case rather than by product comparison.

8.1.heading: Core Business Processes and Organizational Value Chains

qualifications: The supply chain is called a chain for convenience; the chapter says plainly that the accurate picture is a network, because each tier has many suppliers of its own.

Upstream means towards raw materials and downstream means towards the end customer. One firm's order-to-cash overlaps the next firm's procure-to-pay, so the same transaction is a sale on one side and a purchase on the other.

The bullwhip effect is amplification of order variability moving upstream. It is a consequence of each tier reacting to its own order book rather than to end demand; it is not a claim that any tier behaved irrationally.

Customizing an ERP module is costly to maintain because each vendor release must be re-fitted to the changed code. The chapter says costly rewriting, not that an updated module becomes impossible to patch.
A productivity dip shortly after go-live is common and expected while people learn a new process. Treating every dip as proof the system was wrong is as mistaken as treating it as proof of nothing.
Blockchain makes an existing record hard to alter after it is written. It cannot supply a field nobody captured, and the chapter's own treatment spends most of its length on the limits.
Best-of-breed is a real strategy the chapter describes, not a wrong answer. Its cost is that integration is built and maintained per pair of systems.
Framework applications in 8.6 and 8.7 are analytical extensions. A system that improves a firm's position does not by itself change an industry's structure.
